---
title: "3. Version Control"
subtitle: "Commit often, commit clearly"
filters:
  - reading-time.lua
---

Version control with Git is the single most valuable habit you can build as a researcher. It is your unlimited undo button, your collaboration tool, and your evidence trail — all in one.

## The basic cycle in Positron

Every working session follows the same pattern:

::: {.timeline}

::: {.timeline-item}
**Work** — write code, analyse data, edit your manuscript in Positron
:::

::: {.timeline-item}
**Stage** — in the Source Control panel, click **+** next to the files you changed to stage them
:::

::: {.timeline-item}
**Commit** — write a clear message describing what you changed, click the **tick**
:::

::: {.timeline-item}
**Sync** — click **Sync** to push your commits to GitHub
:::

:::

That is it. Repeat every time you finish a meaningful piece of work.

## Writing good commit messages

A commit message should answer: *"What did I change and why?"*

**Good commit messages:**
```
"added linear model for shelter preference"
"fixed figure 3 axis label — was showing mm not cm"
"updated methods section after reviewer comment 2"
"added raw data for shoreline survey round 3"
"removed outlier tank 7 — equipment malfunction noted in fieldbook"
```

**Bad commit messages:**
```
"update"
"fix"
"changes"
"asdfgh"
"final version 3"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
### How often should I commit?
Commit whenever you have done something you would not want to redo. In practice this usually means at the end of every working session, or whenever you finish a discrete piece of work (writing a new analysis, finishing a section of the manuscript, adding new data).
:::

## What to track and what to ignore

Not everything belongs in version control. Your `.gitignore` file tells Git what to skip.

**Track these:**
- All `.qmd` files (your analysis and manuscript)
- `_quarto.yml` and `styles.css`
- `renv.lock` (package versions)
- `references/references.bib`
- `README.md`
- Small derived data files (CSVs under ~10 MB)
- R model objects (`*.rds`) if small enough

**Ignore these:**
- `data/raw/` large files — upload directly to Zenodo instead
- `outputs/` generated files — these are reproduced by rendering `analysis.qmd`
- `_freeze/` Quarto cache
- `.Rhistory`, `.RData`, `.Rproj.user/`
- Any file containing passwords, API keys, or personal information

A good starting `.gitignore` for a Quarto/R project:

```
# R
.Rhistory
.RData
.Rproj.user/

# Quarto
_freeze/
_site/
docs/
/.quarto/

# Large data files
data/raw/*.csv
data/raw/*.xlsx
*.zip

# renv cache (the lockfile is tracked, not the library)
renv/library/
renv/staging/

# OS files
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
```

## Using branches (optional but useful)

If you are making a big change you are not sure about — like trying a new statistical approach — you can create a branch so your main version stays safe.

In Positron, click the branch name in the bottom left corner → **Create new branch**.

Name it something descriptive like `try-mixed-model` or `reviewer-revisions`.

When you are happy with the changes, merge the branch back into main. If it does not work, just delete the branch — your main version is untouched.

::: {.callout-note}
### For most PhD projects, one branch is enough
Branching is more useful for collaborative software projects. For a solo research project, committing to `main` with good commit messages is perfectly fine. Do not over-engineer this.
:::

## Recovering from mistakes

This is where version control earns its place. If you break something:

**Undo the last commit (keep changes):**
In Positron Source Control panel → `...` menu → **Undo Last Commit**

**Revert a file to its last committed state:**
Right-click the file in Source Control → **Discard Changes**

**Go back to an earlier version:**
In Positron, open the Timeline panel (View → Open View → Timeline) to see the history of any file and restore an earlier version.

## Working with co-authors

Everything above works the same with co-authors — coordinating changes across people is the whole reason Git exists. A few things change once you're not working alone:

### Add them as collaborators
On GitHub: repo → **Settings** → **Collaborators** → **Add people**, using their GitHub username or email. They can now clone the repo and push commits directly, same as you.

### Avoid stepping on each other
- **Sync (pull) before you start working** each session — in Positron's Source Control panel, click **Sync** to pull down anyone else's changes before you add your own.
- Split responsibility where you can (e.g. one person on Methods, another on Discussion) — two people editing the same section at the same time is the main source of conflicts.
- If Git reports a **merge conflict**, Positron shows you the conflicting lines directly in the editor — choose which version to keep (or combine them), then stage and commit as normal.

### For larger teams, use branches properly
For three or more active collaborators, or more experimental work, give each person their own branch (see [Using branches](#using-branches-optional-but-useful) above) instead of everyone committing straight to `main`. GitHub **pull requests** add an optional review step before merging a branch in, if you want one.

### List everyone on Zenodo
When you reserve or publish your Zenodo record (chapter 4), add every co-author under **Creators** with their name and, ideally, their [ORCID](https://orcid.org) iD — this is what makes the permanent archived record credit everyone correctly, not just whoever happened to click upload.

::: {.callout-tip}
### What's an ORCID?
A free, permanent researcher ID (orcid.org) that disambiguates your name from others and links your work across journals, Zenodo, and funders. Get one if you don't have one, and ask co-authors for theirs before publishing the Zenodo record.
:::

## Optional: verify reproducibility with GitHub Actions

The template ships `scripts/generate_evidence.R`, which walks every
`fig-`/`tbl-` label cited in `index.qmd`, traces it back through
`analysis.qmd` to the reads/writes and code that actually produced it, and
writes the result to `evidence.json`. Platforms like
[ScienceEcosystem](https://scienceecosystem.org) can read this manifest to
show a reader exactly what generated a given number — not just link to the
repo in general.

Running it locally (`Rscript scripts/generate_evidence.R`) proves your code
still produces those claims *on your machine*. Running it in **GitHub
Actions** on every push proves it on a clean checkout with nothing but what's
committed — the actual claim a "reproducible" badge is making. Don't wire
this up before `renv.lock` exists (Day 1 checklist, previous chapter) — a
workflow with no lockfile to install from just fails on every push.

Once `renv.lock` is committed, add `.github/workflows/reproduce.yml`:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  reproduce:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2
      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
      - run: quarto render analysis.qmd && quarto render index.qmd
      - run: Rscript scripts/generate_evidence.R
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: evidence
          path: evidence.json
```

This is optional. Rendering and archiving on Zenodo (next chapter) works
exactly the same whether or not you set this up — it's an extra layer of
proof, not a requirement.

::: {.callout-note}
### Known limitations
`generate_evidence.R` does static text analysis of R chunks, not real
data-flow analysis — it reads variable assignments and file paths, it
doesn't execute your code to trace them. It's R-only (no Python/Julia
chunks), and can't always tell apart two unrelated chunks that happen to
reuse the same short, generic variable name. These are documented in detail
in the script's own header comment — read it before relying on the output
for anything you haven't spot-checked.
:::

## GitHub as a backup

Every time you sync to GitHub, you have a complete backup of your project in the cloud. If your laptop dies, floods, or gets stolen the day before you submit, you can clone your repository onto any computer and pick up exactly where you left off.

```bash
# Clone your repository onto a new computer
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/koura-habitat-mesocosm
```
